analysis.one_liner: Restores federal bailout assistance for banks' derivatives-trading arms, undoing Dodd-Frank's swap pushout rule.
analysis.headline: The House Financial Services Committee approved the bill in May 2012, but it never received a House floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: Dodd-Frank's Section 716 bars federal bailout help for swaps businesses housed inside banks that enjoy federal deposit insurance. As introduced, this bill repealed that ban outright. The committee rewrote it to keep the ban on paper but carve out broad exceptions — allowing insured banks to keep hedging, most swap dealing, and certain asset-backed-security swaps inside the bank — and to exempt overseas swap dealing entirely.
analysis.who_benefits: Large banks and swap dealers, and the U.S. branches of foreign banks. They could keep derivatives trading inside federally insured depository institutions and regain eligibility for federal assistance if a crisis hit those businesses. Foreign-based swap operations of U.S. banks would be exempt from the prohibition altogether.

how_it_helps.text: The bill replaces Section 716's ban on federal assistance to swaps entities with a rule that lets a covered depository institution keep its federal assistance eligibility while engaging in hedging and virtually all swap activity other than 'structured finance swaps.'
It exempts entirely any swap or security-based swap activity conducted outside the United States with a non-U.S. counterparty by a non-U.S. swaps entity.
It extends the term 'covered depository institution' to uninsured U.S. branches or agencies of foreign banks, bringing them into the same carve-out framework.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers and the deposit insurance funds. If a bank's swaps business runs large losses in a crisis, the federal government — and ultimately taxpayers — could again be called on to absorb them, the exact scenario Section 716 was written to prevent after the 2008 rescues of AIG and other swap counterparties.

drawbacks.text: The bill would restore federal bailout exposure for banks' derivatives losses. Section 716 was enacted precisely so that taxpayers would not again backstop swap dealing of the kind that forced the 2008 rescues of AIG and other swap counterparties.

The committee rewrite softens what its own title promised: instead of repealing the ban, it keeps it nominally but builds exceptions wide enough that a bank engaged in ordinary hedging and non-structured swap dealing would keep bailout eligibility.

A good-faith objection supporters would raise: the pushout rule can push swap dealing from regulated, supervised banks into less-transparent affiliates, and may raise hedging costs for commercial end-users. The bill addresses that concern at the price of re-exposing taxpayers to swap losses.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — lower hedging costs and simpler bank organization — is real but narrow, and it comes at the cost of the core taxpayer protection Congress wrote after the 2008 crisis. The carve-outs are broad enough that the ban would rarely bind, which is why the bill's plain effect is to undo Section 716's central promise while keeping its title.

outcome.mechanism: The House Financial Services Committee approved it, the Agriculture Committee's hold was discharged, it sat on the House calendar — but House leaders never brought it to the floor for a vote before the Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Nan Hayworth introduced the bill on May 11, 2011 as a straight repeal of Dodd-Frank Section 716, the provision barring federal bailout assistance to swap dealers and major swap participants.

The House Financial Services Committee's subcommittee forwarded an amended version on a 21-12 vote, and the full committee ordered it reported by voice vote, reporting it amended on May 11, 2012 as H. Rept. 112-476.

The committee rewrite replaced the full repeal with a revision of Section 716: banks keeping their swap activity to hedging, non-structured finance swaps, and certain asset-backed-security swaps would remain eligible for federal assistance, and foreign swap activity would be exempt entirely.

The House Agriculture Committee, which held jurisdiction over parts of the bill, repeatedly extended its review — May 30, July 16, September 14, and November 16, 2012 — before being discharged on November 16, 2012, when the bill was placed on the Union Calendar.
The bill never received a House floor vote before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013, so Dodd-Frank's prohibition on federal assistance to swaps entities remained law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never passed, Dodd-Frank's bailout prohibition stayed in force: swap dealing that would have been re-allowed inside insured banks had to remain outside them, and taxpayers kept the protection. Banks and swap dealers, who would have gained from the carve-outs, got nothing from this Congress.

for.name: Rep. Nan Hayworth
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 11, 2011 as a repeal of Section 716's bailout prohibition; the bill advanced through committee under her sponsorship.

for.name: House Financial Services Committee
for.what_they_did: Held markups on February 16, 2012, ordered the bill reported amended by voice vote, and reported it on May 11, 2012 (H. Rept. 112-476), rewriting the full repeal into broad carve-outs.

for.name: Subcommittee on Capital Markets and Government Sponsored Enterprises
for.what_they_did: Held a hearing in October 2011 and forwarded the amended bill to the full committee on November 15, 2011 by a 21-12 vote.

for.name: Large banks and swap dealers
for.what_they_did: Lobbied Congress to loosen or repeal Section 716's ban on federal assistance to swaps entities, a stated industry priority after Dodd-Frank.

against.name: House leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a House floor vote; it sat on the Union Calendar (Calendar No. 508) until the Congress ended.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill through four successive extensions of its referral (May 30 to November 16, 2012) before being discharged, keeping it off the floor for six months.

sides.party_line_note: Every member of record backing the bill was a Republican — its sponsor and the Republican-led Financial Services Committee, whose subcommittee advanced it 21-12 and whose full committee reported it by voice vote, with no Democratic cosponsors.

industries.note: The bill would let banks keep broad swap businesses inside federally insured depository institutions and keep bailout eligibility, reversing Dodd-Frank's requirement that risky swaps be pushed out of taxpayer-backed units. Its gain comes at the public's expense of renewed bailout exposure.

The bill newly covers uninsured U.S. branches of foreign banks under the prohibition, but gives them the same broad activity carve-outs as domestic banks, so most could continue swapping while keeping federal assistance eligibility.

industries.industry: Overseas derivatives operations of U.S. banks
industries.note: A new subsection exempts entirely any swap activity conducted outside the U.S. with a non-U.S. counterparty, letting banks route swap dealing through foreign entities free of the bailout prohibition's limits.

The bill allows insured banks to trade structured finance swaps on asset-backed securities when hedging, or when regulators authorize the underlying security types — reopening a business tied to the 2008 crisis, though with narrower conditions than a full repeal.
